findings.paper_title: ANNUAL REPORT ON THE TREASURY MANAGEMENT SERVICE AND ACTUAL PRUDENTIAL INDICATORS 2025/26
findings.headline: No new borrowing undertaken, with council citing elevated long-term rates as constraint
findings.detail: The council undertook no external borrowing in 2025/26 despite a Capital Financing Requirement of £74m and external debt of £63m. The council maintained an under-borrowed position, using cash reserves instead. The reason given is the elevated cost of long-term borrowing (PWLB rates peaked above 5%), which the council judged unaffordable.
findings.matters: The decision not to borrow despite capital needs signals that the council views borrowing as unaffordable at current rates and is instead consuming reserves—a short-term strategy that cannot continue indefinitely as reserves deplete.
findings.figures: £0m new borrowing; external debt £63.060m (unchanged); CFR £74.027m; average external investments £49.1m; 1-year PWLB rate was 5.04% at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Due to the elevated cost of borrowing long-term, no borrowing was undertaken during the year.

findings.paper_title: ANNUAL REPORT ON THE TREASURY MANAGEMENT SERVICE AND ACTUAL PRUDENTIAL INDICATORS 2025/26
findings.headline: General Fund balances fell £1.2m to £8.8m, reducing financial cushion
findings.detail: Revenue reserves in the General Fund declined from £10.064m to £8.823m (down £1.241m or 12%). Combined with the 67% depletion of capital receipts, this indicates the council is consuming working capital reserves at a material rate, leaving less buffer for unforeseen pressures.
findings.matters: Lower revenue reserves reduce financial resilience and the council's ability to absorb unexpected cost pressures, changes in income, or delays in savings delivery.
findings.figures: £10.064m (31 March 2025) to £8.823m (31 March 2026); decline of £1.241m
findings.quote: Balances 10.064 8.823

findings.paper_title: ANNUAL REPORT ON THE TREASURY MANAGEMENT SERVICE AND ACTUAL PRUDENTIAL INDICATORS 2025/26
findings.headline: Usable capital receipts depleted by 67%, falling from £10.6m to £3.5m
findings.detail: The council's usable capital receipts, which originate from the sale of the Golf Course and provide flexible capital finance without borrowing, have fallen dramatically from £10.582m to £3.472m. This sharp depletion significantly constrains the council's ability to fund future capital schemes without recourse to external borrowing.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are the most flexible source of capital finance; their depletion means future capital investment becomes dependent on borrowing at rates the council currently views as unaffordable.
findings.quote: Usable Capital Receipts 10.582 3.472

findings.paper_title: ANNUAL REPORT ON THE TREASURY MANAGEMENT SERVICE AND ACTUAL PRUDENTIAL INDICATORS 2025/26
findings.headline: Forced exit from property fund with £1.12m cumulative valuation loss
findings.detail: In August 2025, Tamworth was compelled to exit the Hermes Federated Property Unit Trust when the fund merged and became restricted to UK pensions only. Since purchase, the property fund investments have fallen in value by £1.12m cumulatively. In 2025/26 alone, valuations fell by £78k. Dividends received in 2025/26 were £276k, down from £442k the previous year.
findings.matters: The forced exit and valuation losses demonstrate difficulty in deploying long-term commercial investments profitably, and indicate limited flexibility in how the council can deploy capital to generate income.
findings.figures: £1.12m cumulative valuation loss; £78k in-year valuation decline; dividends £276k (2025/26) vs £442k (2024/25); total dividends £2.317m since 2018/19 offset against valuation decrease
findings.quote: In August 2025, The Hermes Federated Property Unit Trust merged with L&G's Managed Property Fund and Tamworth Borough Council were not eligible to remain Unit Holders in the new merged fund as this is limited to UK Pensions only.

findings.paper_title: ANNUAL REPORT ON THE TREASURY MANAGEMENT SERVICE AND ACTUAL PRUDENTIAL INDICATORS 2025/26
findings.headline: £23.6m of capital spend re-profiled into 2026/27, signalling delivery delays
findings.detail: Capital expenditure outturn was £17.2m against a budget of £25.3m (32% underspend). The report explicitly notes that £23.6m of planned capital spend has been pushed into 2026/27. HRA capital was particularly affected: £7.3m actual against £15.4m budgeted. The underspend was accompanied by higher-than-expected investment balances as a result.
findings.matters: Material slippage in capital delivery indicates execution risk and suggests the council is struggling to deploy planned investment on schedule, which affects long-term asset condition and service provision.
findings.figures: £23.6m re-profiled; £17.201m actual capital expenditure vs £25.288m budgeted (32% variance); HRA £7.278m actual vs £15.378m budgeted
findings.quote: £23.6m of Capital scheme spend has been re-profiled into 2026/27 (also including re-profiling from previous years) which has increased investment balances.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Internal Audit Quarter 1 2026/27 Progress and Follow-Up of Recommendations Report
findings.headline: Mandatory local government restructure in 2028 will dissolve the borough and merge with five other councils.
findings.detail: Tamworth Borough Council will merge with Lichfield, Stafford, East Staffordshire, Cannock Chase, and South Staffordshire to form a single unitary council from May 2028. The council is also exploring establishing a town council to run alongside this restructure. This represents a major organisational change affecting governance structure and resource management.
findings.matters: Mandatory local government restructuring creates organisational uncertainty and transition risk during a critical period for financial management and service delivery.
findings.figures: 6 councils merging; borough dissolution in May 2028
findings.quote: Tamworth Borough Council will now form a unitary council with Lichfield, Stafford, East Staffordshire, Cannock Chase and South Staffordshire.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Internal Audit Quarter 1 2026/27 Progress and Follow-Up of Recommendations Report
findings.headline: Three corporate high-risk items have not been recently updated or actively assessed.
findings.detail: The council's corporate risk register identifies 10 risks, five of which are rated high-risk. However, three of these high-risk items lack recent assessment: Environmental Investment/Net Zero Sustainability (assessment 9/10/25), Data and Records Management (assessment 3/10/25), and Regeneration/Economic Growth (assessment 9/10/25). This represents a failure to actively monitor and respond to material council risks.
findings.matters: High-risk items not being actively monitored suggest the council may not be identifying or responding to major operational or strategic threats in a timely manner.
findings.figures: 10 corporate risks identified (February 2026); 5 rated as high-risk; 3 high-risk items with outdated assessments from September/October 2025
findings.quote: Risk 6 (Lack of Environmental Investment may compromise Tamworth's Net Zero and Sustainability commitments) – latest notes and assessment 9/10/25.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Internal Audit Quarter 1 2026/27 Progress and Follow-Up of Recommendations Report
findings.headline: Operational risk registers are severely out of date, some not updated for 15 years.
findings.detail: Internal audit found that operational risk registers on the Ideagen system have not been regularly updated. Examples include Asset Management (last assessed June 2010), Community Development (April 2015), Payroll (September 2021), and Castle Grounds (December 2017). In one Directorate, 19 of 25 sub-registers had not been assessed within two years. This was classified as a high-risk finding.
findings.matters: Severely outdated risk registers suggest weak risk identification and monitoring controls across the council, potentially masking emerging operational or financial risks.
findings.figures: Asset Management not assessed since June 2010; Community Development not assessed since April 2015; Payroll not assessed since September 2021; 19 of 25 sub-registers in sample not assessed in 2+ years
findings.quote: Asset Management last assessed, June 2010; Community Development last assessed, April 2015; Payroll last assessed, September 2021

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Internal Audit Quarter 1 2026/27 Progress and Follow-Up of Recommendations Report
findings.headline: Ankerside financial reconciliation is controlled by a single person with no independent review.
findings.detail: Monthly rental income reconciliations for Ankerside are performed by one Finance Team member with no preparer/reviewer separation of duties, no sign-off dates recorded, and no investigation of variances. Internal audit attributed this to recent staffing turnover and resource constraints in the Finance Team.
findings.matters: Absence of segregation of duties in financial controls creates fraud and error risk in managing a material council asset.
findings.figures: Single Finance Team member responsible; recent staffing turnover and recruitment
findings.quote: due to resource constraints and changes to the Finance Team there has not been a segregation of duties for this control. A preparer and reviewer signature as well as date is not included in the reconciliation template.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Internal Audit Quarter 1 2026/27 Progress and Follow-Up of Recommendations Report
findings.headline: Ankerside shopping centre management contracts remain unsigned and roles are unclear.
findings.detail: The council acquired Ankerside in December 2024 to prevent liquidation. The contract with New River (operations manager) remains unsigned due to terminology changes, and the inherited Knight Frank contract (facilities and income management) is not tailored to the current arrangement and does not clearly outline roles and responsibilities. Internal audit classified this as a high-risk finding.
findings.matters: Unsigned or unclear management contracts for a material council asset create operational and legal risk, particularly given the circumstances of the acquisition.
findings.figures: December 2024 ownership takeover; acquisition to prevent liquidation; ~25% shop vacancy in 2024
findings.quote: The Knight Frank contract was inherited by the previous Ankerside owners. This is not tailored to the new set up with the Council as an owner and the involvement of New River and therefore does not clearly set out the roles and responsibilities of Knight Frank within the new arrangement.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Quarter 1 2026/27 Progress and Follow-Up of Recommendations Report
findings.headline: 22% of audit recommendations are overdue with several extremely overdue
findings.detail: Of tracked audit recommendations: 37% are complete, 28% not yet due, 13% in progress, and 22% are overdue. The report explicitly notes that several recommendations are extremely overdue. Senior managers are being asked to address these delays, and the committee is considering requesting the responsible owners of the most overdue recommendations to attend the next meeting to explain the delays.
findings.matters: A substantial backlog of unimplemented audit recommendations indicates the council is slow to address identified control weaknesses and governance issues.
findings.figures: 22% overdue; 13% in progress; 37% complete; 28% not yet due
findings.quote: 28% of recommendations are not yet due; 37% are complete; 13% in progress; and 22% are overdue. Several recommendations are extremely overdue, and the Follow Up report is to be presented at Corporate Management Team on 4th August for Assistant Directors to address any recommendations that fall within their service area.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Quarter 1 2026/27 Progress and Follow-Up of Recommendations Report
findings.headline: Procurement audit added due to governance gaps around compliance and financial guidance
findings.detail: A Procurement audit has been added to the 2026/27 plan at the request of the Executive Director Finance and Commercial (S151 Officer) and Executive Director Housing and Communities. The request stems from concerns about the council's awareness of Procurement Act requirements and adherence to its Financial Guidance. The audit will cost £6.5k and will be funded from existing Internal Audit budgets.
findings.matters: Compliance gaps in procurement and financial guidance represent control weaknesses that could expose the council to legal risk, waste, and financial loss.
findings.quote: A Procurement audit has been requested by the Executive Director Finance and Commercial (S151 Officer) and the Executive Director Housing and Communities due to concerns about awareness of the requirements of the Procurement Act and the Council's Financial Guidance.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: Planning application fee income £32k below budget, attributed to depressed housing applications nationally.
findings.detail: Planning application income underachieved by £31,695k against a budget of £175,270k, with the report attributing this to nationally depressed housing applications. This income line is volatile and difficult to forecast but represents a loss of discretionary income at a time when the council is already running a structural deficit and cannot absorb loss of income.
findings.matters: Planning fees are a proxy for development activity and economic confidence. A significant underachievement flags economic weakness in the area and loss of income the council was counting on.
findings.figures: Planning application fees: budget £175,270k, actual £143,575k, underspend £31,695k (18% shortfall). Reason: 'Housing applications numbers are depressed nationally'.
findings.quote: Housing applications numbers are depressed nationally, which is contributing to our underachievement of income budget.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: Refuse joint arrangement cost increased by £581k, partially offset by reduced recycling credits.
findings.detail: Tamworth's contribution to Lichfield DC's waste service jumped to £2.426m from a budget of £1.845m (£581k overspend), reflecting increased service costs. This was partially offset by lower recycling credits from Staffordshire County Council (£430k reduction in credits received, down to £430k from £1.125m budgeted). Government transition funding for food waste and EPR has been treated as grants in advance, deferring the impact to 2026/27.
findings.matters: Waste is often a volatile cost line, exposed to commodity prices and contractor pricing. A sudden £581k increase signals either contract price escalation or higher tonnage. The deferral of waste transition funding to 2026/27 means the council faces a cliff-edge cost in the coming year.
findings.figures: Refuse joint arrangement overspend £581,555k (budget £1.844m vs. actual £2.426m). Recycling credits received below budget: £430,881k received vs. £1.125m budgeted. Government grants treated as grants in advance: £211,318k (for food waste and EPR transition).
findings.quote: Increased contribution payable to Lichfield DC reflecting cost of service

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: Capital programme 47% underspent (£24.1m reprofiled), signalling project delivery issues.
findings.detail: The General Fund capital budget of £21.219m delivered only £9.923m spend (47% underspend), with £11.269m reprofiled to 2026/27. The HRA capital budget of £20.040m delivered only £7.278m spend (64% underspend), with £12.839m reprofiled. Combined, £24.108m in underspends represents pervasive project delays across both housing and general fund schemes. Appendix C shows delays across street lighting, structural works, heating upgrades, and major roofing programmes, with many noting revised delivery timescales to 2026/27 or beyond.
findings.matters: A lender using capital programme delivery as a proxy for management capability sees a council that is consistently unable to execute its planned works. This raises questions about project management, procurement, and the reliability of future forecasts. It also means assets are deteriorating longer than planned.
findings.figures: General Fund capital: budget £21.219m, spend £9.923m, variance £11.296m (47% underspend). HRA capital: budget £20.040m, spend £7.278m, variance £12.763m (64% underspend). Total reprofiling £24.108m.
findings.quote: The provisional outturn on capital schemes spend is £9.923m (£10.576m projected at period 11) compared to a full year budget of £21.219m (this budget includes re-profiled schemes from 2024/25 of £17.426m). It is requested that £11.269m be re-profiled into 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: CPI inflation forecast in MTFS (2.8%) is now expected to reach 4%, adding to budget pressure.
findings.detail: The medium-term financial strategy was built on a CPI inflation forecast of 2.8%. The outturn report now indicates that CPI could rise to 4% by year end, significantly higher than assumed. This will feed through to contract inflation, energy costs, and demand-driven services across the budget, and comes at a time when the council is already running a structural deficit.
findings.matters: In a tight budget environment with little room for variance, CPI tracking 40% above forecast means the council has a shortfall it cannot absorb. The cost-of-living crisis is explicitly noted as impacting collection performance on council tax and rents.
findings.figures: MTFS assumed 2.8% CPI; indications that CPI could reach 4% by year end.
findings.quote: A CPI inflation rate of 2.8% was assumed in the MTFS forecasts, however, indications are that this could be significantly higher, possibly up to 4% by the year end.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: Pay award will escalate beyond budget: employers offered 3.3% but MTFS assumed 3%.
findings.detail: The MTFS was built on a 3% pay award assumption. Local government employers have offered 3.3%, which the report says is certain to incur additional costs. This applies both to the base pay uplift and cascading increases in employers' NI and superannuation. The trades unions have rejected the offer for non-chief officers, suggesting further pressure is likely.
findings.matters: Pay is typically 50–60% of local authority revenue costs. A 0.3% underestimation on a large base, plus NI and pension uplift, can rapidly exceed budget. The council's narrow revenue margins make this material.
findings.figures: Assumed 3% pay award in MTFS; employers offered 3.3% (accepted for chief officers, rejected by unions for other staff). Includes additional employers' NI and superannuation cost on top.
findings.quote: The MTFS included provision for a pay award of 3% for staff in 2026/27, however, local government employers have offered 3.3%, which, whilst accepted for chief officers, has been rejected by the trades unions at this stage for other staff. It is therefore certain that additional salaries costs will be incurred, including an increased employers' NI and superannuation cost on top of this.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation costs are yet to be quantified but certain to materialize over the next two years.
findings.detail: The report notes that significant additional resources—staffing, consultancy support, and legal advice—will be required to progress local government reorganisation (LGR) and community governance review projects over the next two years. These costs have not yet been quantified and sit outside the current MTFS, adding to future budget pressure at a time when the council is already structurally in deficit.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility on all material future costs. Unquantified LGR costs during a period of structural deficits represent a double pincer: the council is already running out of reserves while facing unknown additional calls on those reserves.
findings.figures: No quantified cost yet provided. LGR to conclude over next two years.
findings.quote: Additional resources including staffing, potential consultancy support and legal advice will be required to progress with local government reorganisation and community governance review projects over the next two years, which are yet to be quantified.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: Universal credit tenants in arrears at 42.3% of council tenants, creating a rent collection risk.
findings.detail: The percentage of council tenants on universal credit who are behind with rent has increased from 40.4% in the prior year to 42.3%. The overall rent arrears increased by £9k year-on-year to £467k (excluding former tenants), and total arrears including former tenant arrears reached £2.316m, up £113k. The council recorded only three evictions since April 2025, suggesting enforcement is not keeping pace with arrears growth.
findings.matters: Rent is a key council revenue source, and a lender is exposed to collection risk if the council's largest tenant population is increasingly unable to pay. UC tenants are systemically vulnerable to income shocks.
findings.figures: 42.3% of council tenants on UC in arrears (prior year 40.4%). Rent arrears (excl. former tenants) £467k, up £9k. Total arrears £2.316m, up £113k. UC claimants in Tamworth increased to 11,591 (from 10,815 prior year).
findings.quote: Currently, 42.3% of universal credit claimants who are council tenants are behind with their rent (40.4% at the end of March 2025).

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Provisional Outturn and Financial Healthcheck
findings.headline: Budgets are currently being balanced by the use of reserves and balances which is not sustainable.
findings.detail: The council's three-year MTFS shows a significant deficit emerging from 2026/27, increasing over the settlement period. The report explicitly warns that reserves are being used unsustainably to bridge a structural gap, and savings of approaching £3.5m per year will be required from 2029/30 onwards to balance budgets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can service debt from operations or is in a managed decline mode. Unsustainable reserve-draining means the council is consuming its financial buffer rather than living within its means.
findings.figures: General Fund balances £9.804m at year-end (increased by £1.050m from budget). Savings approaching £3.5m per year required from 2029/30. Three-year settlement to 2028/29, after which deficits accelerate.
findings.quote: Budgets are currently being balanced by the use of reserves and balances which is not sustainable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Council must continue using reserves to balance budget as structural funding pressure persists

The council requires use of balances and reserves to deliver balanced budgets despite maximizing council tax increases to 2.99%. From 2026/27, the business rates reset will redistribute retained growth to councils with adult social care responsibilities, requiring further financial adjustments.
findings.matters: Ongoing reliance on reserves to balance budgets is unsustainable and indicates a structural deficit that cannot be addressed through tax increases alone

findings.detail: A high-significance finding in the Social Housing Regulatory Programme audit noted non-compliance with the Decent Homes Standard, indicating housing stock does not meet regulatory requirements for condition.

findings.figures: 8 Medium, 2 Low recommendations; Limited assurance on control design

findings.detail: Of 31 outstanding recommendations from prior audits, 17 had surpassed their original implementation date. BDO escalated this to the Corporate Management Team. A common issue was that original action owners had left, and recommendations were not reassigned.
findings.matters: Overdue audit actions indicate the council is not fixing identified control weaknesses; a lender needs confidence that discovered problems are actually being remedied
findings.figures: 31 outstanding recommendations from audits between 2021 and 2026; 17 in progress or overdue
findings.quote: The number of recommendations, and length of time the recommendations have been outstanding is more than would be expected

findings.paper_title: Appendix A TMSS
findings.headline: Council maintaining under-borrowed position, betting on falling interest rates, with no new borrowing planned across 2026/27-2028/29 despite rising capital financing requirement.
findings.detail: The council has a capital financing requirement (CFR) of £81.319m in 2026/27 but only £63.060m in external debt. The under-borrowing position reaches £18.259m in 2026/27 and grows to £21.821m by 2028/29. The strategy relies on current forecasts that interest rates will fall. The treasury advisor notes that 'Bank Rate remains relatively elevated in 2026 even if some rate cuts arise' but the council is still postponing borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about the risk of this strategy if interest rate forecasts prove wrong. If rates do not fall as expected, the council may face higher borrowing costs later. The strategy also depends on continuing to have sufficient cash reserves to cover the CFR without borrowing.
findings.quote: This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels, albeit only once prevailing inflation concerns are addressed by restrictive near-term monetary policy. That is, Bank Rate remains relatively elevated in 2026 even if some rate cuts arise.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A TMSS
findings.headline: Growing Housing Revenue Account debt burden, with debt per dwelling projected to reach £20,172 by 2028/29, up from £17,501 in 2024/25.
findings.detail: HRA debt is increasing steadily across the planning period. The ratio of HRA debt to revenues is 300% in 2024/25, rising to 306% in 2026/27 and holding at 306% by 2028/29. Debt per dwelling rises from £17,501 to £20,172 over the four-year period. The council's HRA is increasingly leveraged.
findings.matters: Lenders use HRA debt ratios to assess housing finance sustainability. A 306% ratio and growing per-dwelling debt suggests increasing pressure on tenant rents and reduced financial flexibility for the housing service.
findings.quote: HRA Debt to Revenues Ratio Actual 300% [2024/25], Estimate 306% [2026/27]. HRA Debt per Dwelling £'000 2024/25 17.501, 2028/29 20.172

findings.paper_title: Appendix A TMSS
findings.headline: Council reserves declining by £20.6m over four years, from £43.8m to £23.1m, as the council uses reserves to fund capital projects.
findings.detail: The council's Fund Balances and Reserves are projected to fall significantly: from £43.774m in 2024/25 to £28.492m in 2026/27, reaching £23.119m by 2028/29. This decline reflects the council's strategy of using internal reserves to finance capital expenditure rather than borrowing externally. Total core funds available for investment fall from £58.736m to £25.288m.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about deteriorating financial resilience. Falling reserves reduce the council's buffer for unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls, and constrain future borrowing capacity.
findings.quote: Year End Resources 2024/25 Actual £43.774m, 2026/27 Estimate £28.492m, 2028/29 Estimate £23.119m. Expected Investments 65.154m [2024/25] to 16.523m [2028/29]

findings.paper_title: Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation into unitary structure from April 2028 creates execution risk on savings plan
findings.detail: The council is likely to merge into a larger unitary authority from 1st April 2028 — a restructuring that will require significant management time and resources to implement. The council has established a Project Management Office for reorganisation planning. This 18-month window (from April 2026) coincides exactly with the period when the council needs to identify and deliver £1m+ annual savings to rebalance the budget.
findings.matters: Reorganisation diverts senior management attention from operational efficiency at precisely the time the council needs to execute a major savings programme. The dual agenda creates execution risk: either reorganisation slips and delays necessary action, or the savings agenda suffers.
findings.figures: Unitary merger effective 1st April 2028; PMO established for reorganisation; £1m savings required from 2027/28
findings.quote: Pending local government reorganisation will also bring challenges and involve significant additional resources to implement. The need for a Project Management Office has been reflected in the budget pressures.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Government changed business rates funding methodology mid-MTFS process, creating planning uncertainty
findings.detail: The council's MTFS was drafted on the basis of the Government's provisional settlement published in December 2025. On 9th February 2026 — after Cabinet and scrutiny review — the Government announced significant changes to the methodology for distributing retained business rates through pooling, with material impact to Tamworth. This late change came after the budget had been through formal scrutiny.
findings.matters: Late policy changes create budget risk. The MTFS may need revision. Tamworth's funding position depends on Government decisions over which it has no control, and precedent shows these can shift with little notice.
findings.figures: Provisional settlement December 2025; final settlement announcement with methodology changes 9th February 2026
findings.quote: This contained some significant changes to the figures published in the provisional settlement in December, which had formed the basis for reports to Cabinet and Joint Scrutiny (Budgets) in January. This included a change in the methodology for distributing retained business rates

findings.paper_title: Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: General Fund reserves will be drawn down by £1.1m in 2026/27, beginning pattern of depletion across MTFS
findings.detail: The council is applying £1,096,790 from General Fund reserves to balance the 2026/27 budget. Across the forecast period to 2028/29, reserves continue to be drawn down each year. While the council will maintain minimum balances of £500k through to 2028/29, the underlying position is that current revenue and expenditure cannot be balanced without reserve support.
findings.matters: Sustained reserve drawdowns indicate the council is living beyond its means on a recurring basis. This erodes financial flexibility and reduces capacity to respond to unexpected demands or income shocks.
findings.figures: £1,096,790 transfer from General Fund Revenue Balances in 2026/27; reserve drawdowns continuing across 2027/28, 2028/29 to cover ongoing deficits
findings.quote: the sum of £1,096,790 be transferred from General Fund Revenue Balances in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: General Fund has structural deficit requiring £1m annual savings from 2027/28 to avoid reserve depletion
findings.detail: The council faces deficits in every year of the forecast period. Reserve drawdowns can cover these in the short term but are unsustainable beyond 2028/29. The MTFS explicitly states that to balance the budget from 2027/28 onwards, the council must identify and deliver £1m+ in annual savings. These savings have not yet been identified.
findings.matters: Unidentified, undelivered savings are red flags for lenders. A £1m annual saving from a General Fund budget of £12.6m is material. Whether the council can find and deliver this by 2027/28 — while managing reorganisation — will determine financial stability.
findings.figures: Net Cost of Services £12,573k in 2026/27; General Fund deficit of £1,096k covered by reserve transfer; savings of at least £1m per year required from 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: Whilst this can be met from General Fund reserves over the short term, savings of at least £1m per year are required from 2027/28 in order to balance the budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 TMSS
findings.headline: Under-borrowing strategy explicitly depends on cash reserves; no contingency if rates don't fall as forecast
findings.detail: The Council states it is 'using cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow as a temporary measure' instead of borrowing. The strategy acknowledges this is prudent only 'as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall'. However, if this forecast proves wrong and the Council has depleted reserves (falling to £23m by 2028/29), it will be forced to borrow at higher-than-forecast rates with minimal financial buffer.
findings.matters: The Council's financial stability over the forecast period is contingent on a specific interest rate outcome. Failure of that outcome leaves no fallback position.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement vs External Debt creates £18.259m gap in 2026/27 funded from reserves. Expected investments £25.596m by 2026/27.
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt, as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 TMSS
findings.headline: HRA debt growing £4.8m in one year with debt-to-revenue ratio at 306%
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account debt rising from £70.507m (2025/26) to £75.312m (2026/27), driven by significant HRA capital expenditure of £12.163m. The debt-to-revenue ratio is 306% in 2026/27 (HRA revenues only £24.615m), up from 300% in 2024/25. This is a high leverage position for a single service area, particularly given the constraints on HRA rent-setting.
findings.matters: High HRA debt ratios reduce financial flexibility and increase vulnerability to rental income shocks or capital cost overruns.
findings.figures: HRA Debt 2025/26: £70.507m, 2026/27: £75.312m, 2028/29: £79.518m. HRA Debt to Revenues Ratio 2026/27: 306%. HRA capital expenditure 2026/27: £12.163m.
findings.quote: HRA Debt £m 70.459 70.507 75.312 77.004 79.518 [2024/25 Actual through 2028/29 Estimate]; Ratio of Debt to Revenues % 300 299 306 305 306

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 Corporate Vision, Priorities Plan, Budget & Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 TMSS
findings.headline: General Fund reserves falling £15.3m in a single year, with accelerating decline forecast through 2028/29
findings.detail: Fund balances declining from £43.774m (2024/25 actual) to £28.492m (2026/27 estimate) to £23.119m (2028/29 estimate). This reflects the Council's strategy of using internal cash reserves rather than borrowing to fund a £81.3m Capital Financing Requirement. Once reserves approach critical levels, the Council will be forced to borrow regardless of interest rates.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand when a council will have no choice but to access debt markets at potentially unfavourable rates, and how thin the buffer for unexpected demand becomes.
findings.figures: Fund Balances/Reserves: £43.774m (2024/25 actual), £28.492m (2026/27 estimate), £23.119m (2028/29 estimate); expected investments fall from £65.154m to £25.596m by 2026/27
findings.quote: Fund Balances/Reserves 43.774 39.851 28.492 25.725 23.119 [Year End Resources 2024/25 Actual through 2028/29 Estimate]

findings.paper_title: Business Rates Income Forecast 2026/2027
findings.headline: Business Rates income estimates will not be confirmed until late January 2026, leaving budget set with unresolved material assumptions
findings.detail: Due to the 2026 revaluation introducing uneven property value shifts across sectors and regions, councils remain uncertain how these changes affect their income. Final estimates are not confirmed until late January—after the budget has been formally approved.
findings.matters: The council is setting its 2026/27 budget without final confirmation of income from a source representing £16.9m of retained cash. Material variance after approval creates mid-year budget pressure.
findings.figures: Estimated yield £42,181,307; authority retained £16,872,523
findings.quote: Councils are still uncertain how these changes will affect their retained income, with business rates income estimates not being confirmed until late January 2026.

findings.paper_title: Business Rates Income Forecast 2026/2027
findings.headline: Appeals risk from 2026 revaluation rated High; expected to increase substantially from economic downturn and pandemic effects
findings.detail: Appeals against new rateable values are categorized as High risk in the council's risk register. The paper states the risk of appeals increases substantially due to current economic climate and Covid aftermath, directly reducing the council's Business Rates income.
findings.matters: Appeals refunds are hard to predict and reduce cash received. High risk means actual income could materially underperform the £42.2m estimated yield.
findings.figures: Estimated yield £42,181,307; appeals risk rated High
findings.quote: the risk of appeals increases substantially due to the current economic climate and the legacy effects of the Covid 19 pandemic

findings.paper_title: Business Rates Income Forecast 2026/2027
findings.headline: Revenue forecast £70,917 below MTFS assumption, showing Business Rates retention baseline has fallen
findings.detail: The authority's retained share after tariff is £2,603,529, but the revised baseline is £2,674,446—a variance of £70,917 shortfall. This represents income the council planned for but will not receive.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's budget balance needs to understand that a major funding source has contracted below planning assumptions, creating a hole that must be filled from reserves or cuts.
findings.figures: Variance (£70,917); baseline £2,674,446; retained share £2,603,529
findings.quote: The revised baseline as notified in the provisional local government settlement is £2,674,446, a variance of £70,917.

findings.paper_title: Business Rates Income Forecast 2026/2027
findings.headline: Business Rates Reset from April 2026 will redistribute income growth since 2013, putting Tamworth's retained business rates income at direct risk
findings.detail: The Business Rates Reset effective April 2026 realigns the baseline and redistributes growth gains accumulated since 2013. The paper explicitly warns that councils which have grown their local business rate base will lose the additional income generated by that growth, directly affecting Tamworth's retained share.
findings.matters: Business Rates is a significant part of the council's core funding (estimated retained £16.9m). This policy redistributes money away from growing councils to others, reducing predictable income.
findings.figures: Authority Retained share £16,872,523 (before tariff); tariff payable £14,268,994
findings.quote: councils that have successfully grown their local business rate tax bases are at risk of losing the additional business rates income generated by that growth

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Property fund portfolio down £1.581m cumulatively since 2021
findings.detail: Property fund valuations have fallen from £10.143m (31 March 2025) to £6.892m (30 September 2025). Cumulative loss since March 2021 is £1.581m. The council was forcibly exited from the Federated Hermes fund when the merged vehicle restricted eligibility to UK pensions, realizing £3.528m from a £4.056m original investment.
findings.matters: Real erosion of financial reserves through underperforming property investments. Forced exit due to fund restructuring demonstrates exposure to investment risks outside the council's control. Cumulative £1.6m loss material to overall reserve position.
findings.figures: Valuation fell from £10.143m (31/03/2025) to £6.892m (30/09/2025); cumulative loss since 2021 of £1.581m; Federated Hermes returned £3.528m on £4.056m original investment
findings.quote: The property fund investment with Federated Hermes has now been returned (our original investment was £4.056m and we received £3.528m, reflecting the current valuation)

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital programme slipping by £5.182m (12.8%) to 2026/27
findings.detail: Of the £40.567m capital budget for 2025/26, only £35.385m is predicted to be spent in-year. The £5.182m slippage defers capital works to 2026/27. Associated borrowing need is also deferred: £1.830m required in 2025/26 against the £4.430m originally budgeted. No explanation is given for the underspend.
findings.matters: Significant capital slippage signals potential delivery issues—either resource constraints, procurement delays, or overly optimistic planning. Deferred infrastructure spending pushes borrowing and its associated costs into the next year, affecting the council's medium-term financial position.
findings.figures: Capital budget £40.567m; predicted outturn £35.385m; slippage £5.182m (12.8% of budget); borrowing need deferred from £4.430m to £1.830m
findings.quote: * Includes potential expenditure slippage into 2026/27 of £5.182m

findings.paper_title: Temporary Reserves and Retained Funds
findings.headline: £1.12m reserve established to protect against property fund value declines
findings.detail: The council has set aside £1.12m specifically to hedge against shortfalls in property fund value, which would otherwise require a charge to the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement. This suggests concern about the valuation of the council's property investments.
findings.matters: Significant exposure to property valuations is material for lenders; if property values fall sharply, the council may have to revalue assets downward and exhaust reserves, or face accounting charges that worsen the financial position.
findings.figures: £1.12m reserve balance; required 'to mitigate effect of any shortfall/reduction in property fund value'
findings.quote: Required in line with requirements of IFRS 9 to mitigate effect of any shortfall/reduction in property fund value which would need to be taken to CIES

findings.paper_title: Temporary Reserves and Retained Funds
findings.headline: Business rates volatility reserve being used to balance budget, with further draws expected in 26/27
findings.detail: The council drew £500k from the business rates reserve in 24/25 to support the balanced budget, will draw another £500k in 25/26, and expects this pattern to continue. The council explicitly notes the fund is 'Likely to be required to balance 26/27 MTFS', indicating non-recurring revenue sources are being used for recurring costs.
findings.matters: Reliance on volatile reserves to balance recurring budgets indicates structural budget pressure; this approach is unsustainable if reserves are depleted or if business rates fall further.
findings.figures: £500k released 24/25, £500k more in 25/26, reserve balance £3.59m
findings.quote: £500k released in 24/25 to support balanced budget and a further £500k contribution will be used in 25/26. Likely to be required to balance 26/27 MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Temporary Reserves and Retained Funds
findings.headline: Ankerside shopping centre consumed £3.97m from reserves in one year despite receiving £1.98m additional funding
findings.detail: The Ankerside shopping centre reserve was drawn down from £2.16m to £0.17m during the year, with £1.98m in additional funding received and still being drawn on. The council retained £170k for 'potential revenue losses/capital investment required', signalling the centre is not generating expected revenue and requires ongoing subsidy.
findings.matters: A major asset requiring sustained capital/revenue subsidy is a risk to the council's financial sustainability; a lender would need to understand whether the shopping centre will ever be self-supporting or if this is an indefinite drain on cash.
findings.figures: £3.97m drawn from Ankerside reserve in 25/26; reserve reduced from £2.16m opening to £0.17m closing despite £1.98m inflow
findings.quote: Required for Ankerside to be used to mitigate potential revenue losses/capital investment required

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure programme has £5.182m slippage (12.8%) into 2026/27, indicating delivery challenges
findings.detail: Total capital budget is £40.567m for 2025/26, but predicted outturn is £35.385m, with £5.182m potential slippage into 2026/27. This represents over one-eighth of the planned programme not executing within the intended financial year, suggesting either delivery weaknesses or significant reprofile of priorities.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage affects cash flow forecasting and may indicate capability gaps in project delivery; for lenders, it signals the speed at which the council can execute its capital strategy and whether investment plans are realistic
findings.figures: Total capital budget £40.567m; predicted outturn £35.385m; potential slippage into 2026/27 £5.182m (12.8% of total)
findings.quote: Includes potential expenditure slippage into 2026/27 of £5.182m

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Gilt yields have risen sharply and strategy explicitly requires ongoing monitoring to avoid elevated longer-dated borrowing costs
findings.detail: PWLB certainty rates have risen materially: 10-year rates moved from 4.70% (1 April) to 5.53% (30 September); 25-year from 5.95% to 6.23%; 50-year from 5.63% to 5.98%. The council is deferring new borrowing by using £12.953m of cash reserves, a prudent tactic that depends on continued low gilt yields. The paper explicitly flags that this strategy requires ongoing monitoring if yields remain elevated, particularly at the longer end of the curve where volatility has been highest.
findings.matters: Sustained elevated gilt yields increase future borrowing costs; the council's current strategy of using cash reserves to avoid new debt is only viable if yields fall as forecast; if they do not, the council will face higher debt servicing costs
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB rates 4.70%–5.53% over period; 25-year 5.95%–6.23%; 50-year 5.63%–5.98%; current internal borrowing £12.953m
findings.quote: This is a prudent and cost effective approach in the current economic climate but will require ongoing monitoring if gilt yields remain elevated, particularly at the longer-end of the yield curve (25 to 50 years).

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Property fund valuations have fallen £1.581m since March 2025, with forced liquidation of Federated Hermes fund at a loss
findings.detail: Tamworth's property fund investments total £6.892m as at 30 September 2025, down from £10.411m at 31 March 2025. The Federated Hermes fund was forced to liquidate after the fund merged and restricted new unit holders to UK Pensions only, leaving Tamworth ineligible. The council received £3.528m on an original investment of £4.056m, realising a loss. Property fund dividend income has also collapsed, from £442k for the full year 2024/25 to only £120k to date in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Lenders assess councils' asset bases and revenue resilience; falling valuations combined with collapsed dividend income both weaken the council's financial position and demonstrate exposure to property market downturns affecting investment returns
findings.figures: Property fund valuations £6.892m (down from £10.411m); Federated Hermes liquidated: £3.528m received on £4.056m invested; dividends £120k to September 2025 versus £442k for full 2024/25
findings.quote: The property fund investment with Federated Hermes has now been returned (our original investment was £4.056m and we received £3.528m, reflecting the current valuation) following the merger with L&G's Managed Property Fund. Tamworth Borough Council were not eligible to remain Unit Holders in the new merged fund as this is limited to UK Pensions only.

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2026/27 To 2030/31
findings.headline: £8m General Fund cost pressures and £4m HRA cost pressures identified across 5-year period, reducing capacity to manage further shocks
findings.detail: New budget pressures totalling £8m for General Fund 2026/27–2030/31 (including £1.58m for 2026/27 alone) and £4m for HRA have been incorporated into forecast. These represent net additions to base costs and reflect service demands, salary commitments, and infrastructure requirements that are now locked in.
findings.matters: Rising committed costs reduce council's flexibility to respond to revenue shocks and worsen underlying deficit position.
findings.figures: GF £1.581m (2026/27), total £8m over 5 years; HRA £775k (2026/27), total £4m over 5 years
findings.quote: Proposed Budget Pressures £8m over 5 years from 26/27... additional cost pressures of £4m over 5 years identified to date in the proposed HRA budget pressures

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2026/27 To 2030/31
findings.headline: Savings delivery plan identified post-Peer Challenge but remains high-level; council has not yet crystallised credible, costed savings programme to close gap
findings.detail: Following Corporate Peer Challenge, council was recommended to develop 'clear savings plan incorporating tangible, costed and deliverable savings'. Council states 'Progress in a number of areas has already been made' but paper shows £8m cost pressures still being added over 5 years, not offset by savings. Financial Resilience Plan exists but actual savings locked in remain unclear.
findings.matters: Council acknowledges need for major savings but has not yet demonstrated credible plan to deliver them; risk of gap persisting and requiring further action later.
findings.figures: £1.4m savings identified for 2025/26; £8m cost pressures added for 2026/27–2030/31
findings.quote: Following the recent Corporate Peer Challenge, and in recognition of the financial challenges the Council faces, it was recommended that the Council develops a clear savings plan incorporating tangible, costed and deliverable savings with robust senior management and member oversight. Progress in a number of areas has already been made

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2026/27 To 2030/31
findings.headline: Local Government reorganisation to potentially create unitary authority from April 2028, adding cost and planning uncertainty to 5-year forecast
findings.detail: Council is required to submit business case for preferred reorganisation option to Government in November 2025. Potential new unitary authority could be in place from April 2028. This introduces further uncertainty and potential one-off reorganisation costs at a time when budget position is already under pressure. Paper notes 'a reserve has been established for limited costs associated which will be kept under review'.
findings.matters: Reorganisation costs will occur during period when council is already in deficit; disruption period could affect service delivery and financial planning; adds volatility to 5-year forecast assumptions.
findings.figures: April 2028 potential implementation date; reserve established but amount unspecified
findings.quote: Further uncertainty has been introduced to the budget process and the MTFS by way of local government reorganisation. We are required to submit a business case for our preferred option for consideration by Government in November with the potential for a new unitary authority to be in place with effect from April 2028

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2026/27 To 2030/31
findings.headline: Commercial and industrial property portfolio income at risk from online retail growth and market decline; council planning increased maintenance spending
findings.detail: Council notes that while commercial/industrial portfolio income 'has held up', there are underlying market risks. Online shopping growth and general retail sector pressure create risk of 'significant loss of income'. Budget proposals include £130.46k increase for commercial building repairs and £192.27k for industrial building repairs, suggesting council recognises deteriorating asset condition.
findings.matters: Portfolio income loss would directly worsen General Fund deficit; increased maintenance spending compounds problem by eating into revenues.
findings.figures: Commercial building repairs increase £130.46k (AST 6 part 1); Industrial building repairs increase £192.27k (AST 6 part 2)
findings.quote: Income from the commercial/industrial portfolio has held up, but underlying market issues and the increase in online shopping mean that there is a risk in relation to the income achievable from the Council's commercial property portfolio, which could result in a significant loss of income

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2026/27 To 2030/31
findings.headline: Ankerside shopping centre requires significant ongoing maintenance spending while tenant income remains uncertain due to retail sector decline
findings.detail: Council identified specific risk that Ankerside shopping centre's income streams are uncertain despite requirement for significant maintenance expenditure. This reflects broader retail decline and online shopping pressure. Council has budget pressures of £62k for Ankerside in 2026/27 for net expenditure and income requirements.
findings.matters: Council holds commercial property with mandatory maintenance costs but declining, uncertain rental income; loss of income or need to increase maintenance would worsen budget position.
findings.figures: £62k Ankerside budget pressure 2026/27 (AST 9 proposal)
findings.quote: there are further risks with regard to the Ankerside shopping centre whereby income streams from tenants are uncertain although significant expenditure is required to maintain the building

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2026/27 To 2030/31
findings.headline: Both General Fund and HRA capital programmes face major funding gaps: GF £2.5m over 5 years, HRA £26m over 5 years
findings.detail: Insufficient capital resources identified to fund proposed schemes. General Fund faces £2.5m shortfall over 5 years (£922k over 3 years) which would have to be funded from revenue, worsening revenue position. HRA capital programme has 'significant' £26m funding gap estimated over 5 years due to stock investment demands and ongoing maintenance requirements.
findings.matters: Deferred capital maintenance increases reactive repair costs and asset deterioration; GF shortfall forces revenue budget further into deficit; HRA gap threatens housing stock quality and compliance.
findings.figures: GF capital shortfall £2.5m (5 years), £922k (3 years); HRA capital gap £26m (5 years); GF CFR £6.992m; HRA CFR £73.057m
findings.quote: insufficient resources are available to finance all of the GF schemes submitted... would mean a £2.5m shortfall over the next 5 years which would have to be funded from revenue and makes the revenue shortfall worse... there will be a significant funding gap for the HRA capital programme – this is currently estimated at £26m over the 5 year period

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2026/27 To 2030/31
findings.headline: HRA debt forecast to become unaffordable in later years despite incorporating £4m of additional cost pressures; 30-year business plan sustainability is unresolved
findings.detail: HRA 30-year business plan shows predicted debt becoming 'unaffordable in later years'. Paper acknowledges 'there is still work to be done to ensure that the HRA remains sustainable into the future'. This is despite £4m cost pressures being built into 5-year forecast. Early modelling of recent Government rent convergence rules indicates improvement but does not fully resolve affordability.
findings.matters: HRA is secured against housing assets; if debt becomes unaffordable, refinancing may be needed or borrowing curtailed, affecting capital investment programme and service delivery.
findings.figures: £4m HRA cost pressures over 5 years; HRA CFR £73.057m 2025/26; HRA balances £3.3m (2026/27), £3.9m (2028/29), £6.0m (2030/31)
findings.quote: whilst this does improve the position, predicted debt still becomes unaffordable in later years and there is still work to be done to ensure that the HRA remains sustainable into the future

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2026/27 To 2030/31
findings.headline: Business Rates Reset and Fairer Funding Review create high-risk funding uncertainty; final grant position not confirmed until December 2025
findings.detail: Government is implementing significant reforms to Local Government funding allocation from 2026/27, including business rates redistribution and fairer funding review. The paper explicitly states this carries 'high risk' that council funding will be 'significantly' affected. Current forecast assumes existing funding levels but acknowledges this assumption may be wrong. Final details expected in draft settlement late December 2025.
findings.matters: Largest source of uncertainty in forecast; council cannot lock in budget until settlement announced; material risk that actual funding is materially worse than forecast.
findings.figures: Forecast RSG £370k 2026/27; assumes 2% annual increase; Business Rates Tariff £12.5m 2026/27
findings.quote: There is a high risk that these reforms will have a significant effect on the Council's funding level from 2026/27. The forecast grant reductions and uncertainty over the impact of the business rates reset and redistribution of Local Government funding puts significant pressure on the ability of the Council to publish a balanced 3 year MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Draft Base Budget Forecasts 2026/27 To 2030/31
findings.headline: General Fund balances forecast to reach £21.5m shortfall by 2030/31, a deterioration of £14.9m from February 2025 forecast
findings.detail: Projected General Fund balances of £4.4m in 2026/27 fall to £8.3m shortfall by 2028/29 and £21.5m shortfall by 2030/31 (including £500k minimum). This is substantially worse than the February 2025 forecast which showed balances of £4.9m in 2026/27 and a £3m shortfall by 2028/29. The deterioration reflects updated base budget pressures and revised assumptions.
findings.matters: A council running deficits of this scale will need to raid reserves or find major savings; inability to balance budgets puts credit quality at risk for lenders and raises refinancing risk.
findings.quote: As a result of the updated base budget, the projections now identify General Fund balances of £4.4m by 2026/27 (compared to £4.9m), a shortfall of £8.3m by 2028/29 (compared to a shortfall of £3m), with a shortfall of £21.5m by 2030/31

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - Tamworth Borough Council- A&G 12-11-2025
findings.headline: Council to be abolished by April 2028 and merged into new unitary authority, creating material structural uncertainty
findings.detail: Tamworth Borough Council will cease to exist by April 2028 under local government reorganisation, with services being merged into a new southern Staffordshire unitary authority. Interim proposals were submitted in March 2025, with full business cases expected late 2025. The council will submit its business case in November 2025. The report identifies challenges around staff integration, systems, service delivery, and maintaining local decision-making.
findings.matters: A major structural change eliminating the council entity by 2028 creates significant uncertainty for medium-term financial planning, loan repayment capacity, and governance continuity
findings.figures: Abolition date: April 2028; Business case submission: November 2025
findings.quote: The Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) proposals will see Tamworth Borough Council abolished by April 2028, with its services likely to be merged into a new southern Staffordshire unitary authority... However, the transition also brings challenges — particularly around maintaining strong local representation, protecting community-focused decision-making, and managing the integration of staff, systems, and service delivery arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - Tamworth Borough Council- A&G 12-11-2025
findings.headline: Prior-year governance recommendation on finance workforce planning remains unimplemented after 12 months
findings.detail: A recommendation from the 2023/24 audit to consider the LGA 'Local government finance workforce action plan for England' has not been completed. Management attributes ongoing delays to completion of the senior management restructure at Assistant Director and Head of Services levels. The LGA CFO Mentoring programme is in train for the Interim Executive Director Finance.
findings.matters: Persistent delays in implementing governance recommendations suggests challenges with management follow-through and capacity planning in the finance function
findings.figures: Recommendation outstanding for 2 audit years
findings.quote: One improvement recommendation made in 2023/24 remains outstanding... Progress has been made in addressing this recommendation; however implementation remains ongoing... Progress is being made in respect of restructure of senior management and around Assistant Director and Executive Director levels. The next level of head of services is currently going through this process. Once this is finalised then the recommendation can be processed.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - Tamworth Borough Council- A&G 12-11-2025
findings.headline: Finance leadership capacity: Assistant Director Finance role vacant since September 2024 in a small team
findings.detail: The AD Finance position has been vacant for 12 months pending completion of the Corporate Management Team restructure and is currently out to advert, though temporary cover was provided. The report acknowledges the finance team is small with reliance on individual members. While management states the team continues to manage effectively, a year-long vacancy in critical finance leadership during a major structural change (LGR) presents a capacity risk.
findings.matters: Finance leadership capacity is essential for loan covenant compliance and managing financial performance; a prolonged vacancy in a small team suggests potential resource constraints during the council's reorganisation transition
findings.figures: 12 months vacancy since September 2024

The Council did have the temporary cover in the interim period. While the size of the finance team means there is some reliance on individual members, the team continues to manage its responsibilities effectively and maintain sound financial oversight across the Council.

news_drafts.headline: No new borrowing undertaken, with council citing elevated long-term rates as constraint
news_drafts.lead: The decision not to borrow despite capital needs signals that the council views borrowing as unaffordable at current rates and is instead consuming reserves—a short-term strategy that cannot continue indefinitely as reserves deplete.

news_drafts.lead: Lower revenue reserves reduce financial resilience and the council's ability to absorb unexpected cost pressures, changes in income, or delays in savings delivery.

news_drafts.lead: Capital receipts are the most flexible source of capital finance; their depletion means future capital investment becomes dependent on borrowing at rates the council currently views as unaffordable.
